analysis.headline: Referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee on February 4, 2025, where it received no further action; it had 1 Republican and 2 Democratic cosponsors alongside sponsor Sen. Bernie Sanders.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cap credit card interest rates at 10% APR, including all finance charges, through January 1, 2031. It would stop lenders from using fees to get around the cap, and it would let borrowers sue to recover any interest, finance charges, or fees they paid above the limit within two years. A lender that knowingly overcharges would forfeit all interest on the debt, and the cap would be enforced under the Truth in Lending Act by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the Federal Trade Commission. State laws offering stronger protections would not be overridden.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that carry a balance on a credit card — tens of millions of Americans who currently pay interest rates well above 10% — would pay less interest each month, and could claw back charges above the cap for two years prior.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on credit cards at 10%, inclusive of all finance charges.
Prevents lenders from loading costs into fees to evade the cap; fees that are not finance charges cannot exceed the total finance charges assessed.

Gives borrowers a private right of action: they can sue within two years to recover interest, finance charges, or fees paid above the limit, and a knowing violation forfeits the entire interest on the debt.

Adds the cap to the Truth in Lending Act's civil liability provisions, enforced by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the Federal Trade Commission, and leaves stronger state consumer-protection laws in place.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers — banks and finance companies that earn interest and fee revenue on card balances — would lose the income from everything charged above 10% APR, which is where most revolving card debt is priced today. Issuers could not shift costs into fees, because the bill caps non-finance-charge fees at the total of finance charges [S3].

drawbacks.text: A hard price cap on credit would likely reduce access for borrowers with weaker credit: lenders who can no longer price for risk may decline those applicants or tighten credit lines rather than lend at 10%, leaving the riskiest borrowers with fewer options.
The cap is temporary — it sunsets on January 1, 2031 — so relief for cardholders would end unless Congress renews it.
Issuers might offset the lost interest revenue by cutting card rewards or raising other charges; the bill anticipates fee-shifting but caps, rather than eliminates, that route.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households carrying credit card debt, the direct benefit is large and immediate: interest charges above 10% would stop, and the recovery and forfeiture provisions give borrowers real leverage. The main cost falls on a concentrated industry — card issuers' interest revenue — which is the point of the bill. The serious tradeoff is on the back end: borrowers with poor credit may find cards harder to get, since lenders can no longer charge rates that offset their risk, and the relief expires in 2031. On balance, the bill delivers substantial, targeted help to indebted households at the expense of issuer profits, with a real but secondary risk of reduced credit access for the least creditworthy borrowers.

outcome.mechanism: Read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on February 4, 2025; no committee markup, floor action, or vote is recorded.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced S. 381 in the Senate on February 4, 2025, joined by Sen. Josh Hawley as an original cosponsor.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The bill attracted 3 cosponsors — 1 Republican and 2 Democrats — and the action history records no further activity after the committee referral.

key_actors.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
key_actors.what_they_did: Introduced S. 381 on February 4, 2025, to cap credit card APRs at 10% through 2031.

key_actors.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
key_actors.what_they_did: Joined Sanders at introduction, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship; he is not counted among the 3 later cosponsors.

key_actors.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
key_actors.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 4, 2025; the action history records no markup, report, or further consideration.

analysis.trajectory: The 119th Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill is technically alive. But rate-cap bills of this kind almost never advance without a committee markup, and the Banking Committee has taken no action in the months since referral; absent an unusual push, the likely path is that it sits without a hearing or vote and dies when the Congress ends.
